findings.subject: While offline, flush returns without writing the draft to the note cache, so reopening the note shows the pre-edit body, and typing there makes schedule delete the queued offline draft, silently losing the offline edit.

A save response for an older draft that arrives after a newer one overwrites the ['note', id] cache with the older body, so reopening the note shows stale text and the next save from that editor sends the older content over the newer server version.

The 401 handler only sets the session to null and leaves the previous account's cached notes, selected note, and queued drafts in place, so a different user who signs in on the same browser briefly sees the previous account's note list and open note body.
A title containing a NUL character passes the string and length checks, Postgres rejects it, and PATCH /api/notes/:id returns a generic 500 instead of a 400 naming the title field.
A body whose text contains a \u0000 escape passes isTipTapDoc, Postgres jsonb rejects it, and PATCH /api/notes/:id returns a generic 500 instead of a 400 naming the body field.
The title input has no maxLength of 500, so a longer title makes every PATCH fail with 400 and the body edits sent with it are never persisted, and they are lost on reload.

errorHandler ignores a 4xx status on non-HttpError errors such as Express malformed-param decode failures (400) and body-parser charset or encoding errors, so a client-caused error returns a 500 and logs as a server fault, contrary to AC-075.

Dashboard calls discardQueuedDrafts before the signed-out editor unmounts, so an unsent draft queued at unmount survives sign-out and is later sent under the next account's session, keeping a beforeunload prompt active.

authenticate() passes the raw submitted password to bcrypt.compare with no length check, and bcrypt silently truncates input at 72 bytes, so for an account whose password is exactly 72 bytes any password sharing that 72-byte prefix (for example the password plus extra characters) signs in, which violates AC-003's requirement that an incorrect password is rejected.

When a query returns 401 the QueryCache onError only sets ['session'] to null and leaves the ['notes'] and ['note', id] caches and the store's selectedNoteId in place, so after a session expires (for example on reconnect) and a different user signs in on the same browser, the new user's Dashboard briefly renders the previous account's note titles and open note body before the refetch returns.

The title check accepts any string up to 500 characters, so a PATCH whose title or body contains a U+0000 character passes validation and then fails at the PostgreSQL text/jsonb insert with an unhandled error, returning a generic 500 on every save and leaving the note permanently unsavable instead of a 400 naming the field.

The save function is never called while offline, so the ['note', id] cache never receives the queued edit; reopening the note shows the stale server body, and the next keystroke in that editor runs queuedDrafts.delete, which discards the queued offline edit permanently.

The save function writes every server response into ['note', id] unconditionally, so a slower earlier save that returns after a newer draft was cached overwrites it with older content, and reopening the note or typing into the stale-mounted editor then saves the older body over the newer one.

A title or body containing U+0000 passes validation, Postgres rejects it (text NUL and jsonb \u0000), and the request returns a generic HTTP 500 instead of a 400 naming the field, so auto-save shows 'Unable to save' for that note and AC-075 is not met.

A malformed percent-encoded note id such as GET /api/notes/%E0%A4%A raises Express's 400 decode error with no body-parser type, which falls through to the generic 500 branch, so the client gets a 500 and the server logs a stack trace instead of a 400 validation response.

A PATCH whose title or body contains a NUL (U+0000) character is passed unvalidated to Postgres, which rejects it in text and jsonb, so the save returns a generic HTTP 500 and the note stays unsaved (the editor shows Unable to save) instead of a 400 naming the field.

Sign-out proceeds even when the pending save failed (flushPendingSave resolves on error), and the editor's unmount then re-queues the previous account's unsent draft after discardQueuedDrafts() has already run, so the leave-page prompt stays active and the stale draft is re-sent under the next session.

validateEmail excludes only whitespace, so an address containing an ESC (U+001B) control character is accepted at registration and is then written unescaped into the server log by the console.info line in requestPasswordReset, letting the registrant inject terminal escape sequences into operator logs.

PATCH /api/notes/:id with a title or body containing a NUL character (\u0000) is rejected by PostgreSQL and returns HTTP 500 with a server-side error log instead of a 400 naming the field, so AC-075 validation handling fails for ordinary invalid client input.

validateEmail accepts a NUL character inside the email, so register and sign-in pass it to PostgreSQL and return HTTP 500 instead of a 400 naming the email field or a 401, which fails AC-075 for that input.

The save function writes each server response into the ['note', id] cache even when a newer draft has been sent, so a slower older response that arrives last replaces the newer content, and reopening the note shows the older body and the next keystroke re-saves it over the newer edit.

handleSignOut calls discardQueuedDrafts before NoteEditor unmounts, and the unmount then re-queues a failed unsent draft, so after sign-out the previous user's note body stays in the module-level queue, the beforeunload prompt keeps firing, and the draft is re-sent on the next online event under the next session.
Session JWTs stay valid for up to 7 days after a password reset or sign-out, so a stolen cookie keeps reading and editing the account's notes after the owner resets the password.
Sign-in has no 72-byte limit while registration enforces one, so bcrypt truncation lets any input whose first 72 bytes equal the stored password sign the user in.

Sign-out calls discardQueuedDrafts before the editor unmounts, so a draft whose save failed is re-queued afterward and is re-sent under the next session on the next online event, while the leave-page prompt stays armed.

Sign-out awaits flushPendingSave, which resolves even when the save failed, so signing out after an "Unable to save" response discards the unsaved edit, and the orphaned draft stays in the module-level queue for the next account in the same tab.

calls.label: opus-medium-1
calls.summary: I found no actionable security defects in the changed code. I traced the main security paths and each matches the plan. Every notes query is filtered by user_id. Session JWTs are HS256 with a pinned algorithm and a check that sub is a string. Cookies are httpOnly, SameSite=Lax and Secure in production. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt and the plaintext is never stored or logged. Reset tokens come from randomBytes and only their SHA-256 hash is stored; they expire after one hour. Unknown emails are compared against a dummy hash, and forgot-password responds without waiting on the lookup. The 500 handler sends only a fixed generic message. SQL is parameterised; the only value placed directly into a query string is a constant. Note ids must be UUIDs and note bodies are type-checked. The toolbar accepts only http, https and mailto links. The reset token is removed from the address bar after it is read. Behaviours the approved plan deliberately chose were not reported: reset tokens are reusable, sign-out does not revoke the token server-side, and the reset link is written to the server log.

calls.label: opus-medium-2
calls.summary: I audited every changed path for security defects and found none to report. Untrusted input reaching the backend is checked: auth and notes body fields must be strings, note ids must be UUIDs, titles are capped at 500 characters and note bodies are type-checked. Every SQL query uses parameters. Every notes query filters by the user id taken from a JWT that is verified as HS256 and must carry a string sub claim. The session cookie is httpOnly and SameSite=Lax, and it is Secure in production. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt at cost 12 and are never logged or returned. Sign-in compares against a dummy hash when the email is unknown, so both outcomes cost one comparison. Reset tokens are 32 random bytes; only their SHA-256 digest is stored, and they expire after one hour. The forgot-password response is the same whether or not the account exists, and the reset is not awaited. Generic 500 responses contain nothing taken from the error, and body-parser errors are answered without logging the request body. Startup configuration errors name the variable without its value and reject the placeholder JWT secret. On the frontend, links set from the toolbar must use http, https or mailto, the reset token is removed from the address bar on first render, and sign-out clears the query cache and queued drafts. Two behaviours were left out because the approved plan chose them: existing sessions stay valid after a password reset, and reset tokens can be reused.

calls.label: opus-medium-3

findings.subject: The QueryCache 401 handler only sets ['session'] to null; it does not clear the other queries or reset the store as the sign-out path does. After user A's session expires or becomes invalid, user B signing in on the same browser immediately sees A's cached ['notes'] list and A's still-selected note ('note', selectedNoteId) in the editor until refetches return 404, which exposes A's note titles and content to B.

calls.summary: Security review of the foundation change found one actionable defect. When a session expires or becomes invalid, the frontend's 401 handler switches to the sign-in screen but keeps the previous user's cached notes and selected note id. A different user who then signs in on the same browser is shown the earlier user's note list and open note before refetches fail. The backend checks were traced and are sound: authentication, password hashing and reset-token handling, per-user filtering on every notes query, cookie options, and generic 500 responses.
